bio.en: Marty Cagan is the author of Inspired and Empowered and a partner at SVPG, who has coached more product teams and PMs than almost anyone, and recently released a new book on modern product practice.
bio.zh: 马蒂·卡根（Marty Cagan）是《Inspired》与《Empowered》的作者、SVPG 的合伙人，他辅导过的产品团队与 PM 几乎无人能及，近期又推出了一本关于现代产品实践的新书。

summary.en: Marty argues many companies overhired during the pandemic, creating fake product roles like agile coaches and product owners that deliver output, not outcomes. He pushes back on the "victim" mindset, insisting individual contributors can drive real change from within. The episode is a bracing call to rediscover what true product management looks like.
summary.zh: 马蒂认为，许多公司在疫情期间过度招聘，制造出敏捷教练、产品负责人等"假产品角色"，它们只交付产出而非成果。他反对"受害者"心态，坚持一线产品人也能从内部推动真正的改变。本期是一次令人警醒的呼吁：重新发现真正产品管理的模样。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: There is no question that a lot of companies overhired during the pandemic. I go into some companies and honestly I can't believe all the ridiculous roles that they have, agile coaches and product owners and product ops and business analysts.
turns.zh: 毫无疑问，许多公司在疫情期间过度招聘了。我去过一些公司，坦白说，我简直不敢相信他们设了那么多荒谬的职位——敏捷教练、产品负责人、产品运营和业务分析师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is essentially the theater you're describing, people that aren't real product managers.
turns.zh: 这基本上就是你所描述的闹剧——那些根本不是真正的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: They're dramatically overpaid for the value they provide. Because it's a project management role. It is a lot easier to deliver output than it is to deliver outcomes.
turns.zh: 他们的薪资远超其所提供的价值。因为这只是个项目管理角色。交付产出要比交付成果容易得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What made you decide to write another book and what is it about?
turns.zh: 是什么促使你决定再写一本书？内容是关于什么的？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Too many people in our industry view themselves as a victim of their company, like they're stuck in a feature team and there's nothing they can do about it other than quit. I think that's not true. There is so much they can do.
turns.zh: 我们行业里太多人把自己视为公司的受害者，好像被困在某个特性团队里，除了辞职就无能为力。我认为这不是真的。他们其实能做很多事。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Thanks very much Lenny. Thanks for inviting me back.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你，莱尼。感谢你再次邀请我来节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you for coming back. So our first episode together is still one of the top five most popular episodes of my entire podcast, which is wild because the podcast was much smaller back then. You've also got a book coming out. We're going to talk about that. You've also been getting a lot more spicy in your writing as of late. You've been writing about product management theater and product leadership theater and all these sorts of things. So I'm excited to dig into a lot of these things. I thought I'd start with just asking what is driving this recent spiciness in your writing?
turns.zh: 谢谢你能回来。我们一起录的第一期节目至今仍是我整个播客节目中最受欢迎的五期之一，这真是令人惊讶，毕竟当时播客规模要小得多。你新书也要出版了，我们今天会聊聊这个。最近你的文章风格变得越来越犀利了，比如写产品管理剧场、产品领导力剧场之类的内容。真期待能深入探讨这些话题。我想先从一个问题入手：是什么促使你最近在写作中变得如此尖锐？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: It's conscious. I find myself, I'm aware of myself dialing up the rhetoric around this stuff. I've actually been saying these things for a long time, honestly, and it's on the record. You can read the blog articles from 10 years ago, 20 years ago, but things are changing. And first of all, I should acknowledge, I don't know if you're this way Lenny, but most product people I know like me are paranoid. So we're always worried that things are going to come and just take our customers away and disrupt our products. And so I know that there's a degree of that. I'm always looking at what are the things that could really shake things up in a good way but also in a bad way? And there's been a number of things I've been very worried about for a long time and I think that there's a convergence of factors that are going on and one of the challenges is it's simultaneous. (00:06:22): So there are a number of things happening in parallel, which is a recipe for some chaos and a lot of fear. And in the product community, in the design community, in the engineering community, it's there. You can see it. And like you, I talk to people pretty much every day. So I do have a lot of theories about why this is going on and what people can do to best protect themselves, their career, their companies. And so I'm happy to share that, but it's not small. It's not a small set. Maybe before I get into it though, I realize that people should understand where I'm coming from and how it's different than where you're coming from because this perspective... Just to be clear, I think we're both trying to help the product community, but we're trying to do it in very different ways. (00:07:18): And I want to be clear, I love the way you do it. In fact, if people don't know, I'm a paid subscriber to yours because I find it incredibly useful for what I want to do. So let's talk about that. You obviously could describe what you do better than anyone, but my take is that you are, and this is what I find valuable, you're sharing a broad range, increasingly broad range of perspectives, people, ways of working, ways of doing products, experiments with the product model, experiments in leadership. I love that. It actually helps me a lot. That's why I subscribe. And I'll be honest, the main reason I took some prodding for me to... I know there's something about actually paying for a subscription when there's a hundred different product related newsletters and stuff, but what happened was you have a lot of subscribers and people that I know would see something and they'd email me and they'd say, "Did you see what Lenny was talking about with Lenny or with whoever? And how do you explain that? What do you think is going on?" (00:08:29): And it made me want to watch a lot of these. Some of companies I know, but other ones you've introduced me to that I don't know anybody at. So to me that's incredibly valuable. It's a whole lot easier than the way it used to be, which is a whole lot of traveling to a lot of companies. So I love that. You are helping so many people to get a broader understanding of product. My goal is different, the SVPG. We are also trying to help the product community, but it's interesting when I watch your interviews, you're trying to pry out of people what's special about what they do, which is what I want to hear. But interestingly, what I'm looking for is not what's different, it's what's the same. What we are all about is sharing the principles and the practices that are used consistently by the best product companies. In fact, we have a heuristic, we've never made a secret of this. (00:09:27): We are always asked about new techniques and new methods, new processes and we're like, "Look, we need to see it being used by at least several of the companies that have proven they can consistently innovate." If those companies can use it productively, we're all about evangelizing that. We make this clear in every one of the books. We don't invent any of these things. We just, if they work, we like to talk about them. So we are looking for the commonality and mostly we're looking to help a company, whether it's a startup or a large company to have the best possible chance of success. That's the goal for us. It's a different goal. You can see that. So all these data points become interesting as data points, but we're looking for those things that last and you never know. You have to see. (00:10:25): For one, I love working with startups, but as you know, a lot of startups are dominated by the founder and the early people and it almost doesn't matter what techniques they use. If they're good, it's amazing what they do. That's just amazing. And so that's probably important to get out of the way.
turns.zh:
这是刻意为之。我发现自己，总是在刻意放大对这些事情的言辞。说实话，我其实很久以前就一直在说这些话，而且这些观点都有记录。你们可以去读十年前、二十年前的博客文章，但如今情况已然不同。首先，我得承认，不知道你是否也这样，但我认识的大多数产品从业者都有些偏执。比如，我们总是担心会有新事物夺走我们的客户，颠覆我们的产品。所以我知道这种担忧是存在的。我一直在思考，哪些因素可能会带来重大变革——无论是积极的还是消极的。长期以来，我一直担忧着许多潜在威胁，而如今这些威胁正叠加交汇，其中最关键的挑战在于它们同时发生。（00:06:22）：多个变革因素并行推进，这无疑会引发混乱与恐慌。在产品社区、设计社区、工程社区，这种焦虑感显而易见。我几乎每天都在与业内人士交流。因此，我对变革背后的原因及应对策略深有体会。（00:07:18）：但首先，我得让大家明白我的立场与你的不同，因为这种视角……说白了，我们都致力于助力产品社区发展，但方法截然不同。（00:08:29）：你无疑能比任何人都更出色地诠释自己的工作，但我认为你的价值在于，你正在分享广泛且日益丰富的视角、人物、工作方式、产品开发理念、产品模型实验以及领导力实践。我深受启发，这正是我订阅你的原因。说实话，在面对数百个产品相关的新闻通讯时，付费订阅可能显得有些多余，但关键在于你拥有大量订阅用户，而我认识的许多人看到相关内容后都会发邮件问：“你看过Lenny或其他人讨论的这个话题吗？你怎么看待这件事？”这促使我去深入了解其中许多公司。有些公司我已熟知，但更多是通过你介绍的陌生团队。因此，这对我极具价值。相较于过去四处拜访各家公司的模式，如今这种学习方式高效得多。我很欣赏这一点。你正在帮助众多从业者拓宽对产品的认知。我的目标有所不同——SVPG（Silicon Valley Product Group）同样致力于助力产品社区，但有趣的是，当我观看你的访谈时，你试图挖掘受访者独特的成功秘诀，而这正是我想听的。但有趣的是，我寻找的并非差异，而是共性所在。我们致力于分享最优秀产品公司始终践行的原则与实践。事实上，我们有一套启发式方法，
这一点我们从不隐瞒。（00:09:27）：总有人问我们新技术、新方法、新流程，我们会说：“看吧，我们得先看到至少有几家能持续创新的公司在实际应用这些东西。”如果这些公司能有效利用这些方法，我们就会积极推广。我们在每一本书里都明确说明这些观点——这些方法都不是我们原创的，只要行之有效，我们就会大力宣传。所以我们的核心工作是寻找共性规律，帮助初创企业或大公司最大限度提升成功概率。这才是我们的目标。我们的目标不同，你们能看得出来。这些数据点本身很有趣，但我们更关注那些经得起时间考验的要素——有些东西一开始看似微不足道，但只有亲眼见证其价值，才能真正领悟其深意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love this.
turns.zh: 是啊，我超爱这个。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Bringing that perspective.
turns.zh: 提出那个观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I agree with everything you said. I think we are very different in what we're providing to the product community. And it's interesting being on this side of the microphone is I built a lot of empathy for journalists. I know the Brian Chesky episode is a good example where there's a lot of things there that might sound problematic and you disagreed with. And as me interviewing him, the challenge I have is I have an hour with him and I have to always decide, do I go and push back and try to, hey, is this actually working the way you're describing? Is this actually the right way to approach stuff? Here's why maybe you would not. Versus there's so many things I want to get to and ask him about this stuff. I'm like, oh, which way do I go? And then if I'm pushing back too hard, people are like, "I'm not going to go on this podcast where he is just questioning everything I think." So it's a really interesting role.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同你说的一切。我觉得我们为产品社区提供的服务截然不同。站在这个麦克风这边很有趣的一点是，我对记者们产生了极大的共情。我知道布莱恩·切斯基那期节目就是个很好的例子，其中有很多听起来可能有问题的内容，而你对此并不认同。作为采访他的人，我面临的挑战是，我只有一个小时的时间和他交流，必须不断权衡：是去反驳他，试图质疑他所描述的做法是否真的有效？是否是正确的处理方式？还是因为我有太多想问他的问题？我就会想，哦，该怎么选？但如果反驳得太猛，人们就会说：“我才不会去参加这个播客呢，他老是质疑我所想的一切。”所以这真是个很有趣的角色。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: I think that's totally fair. And also, I don't think you want to scare off your guests. This is really the platform they have to share what they think is important. I do always find it entertaining because a number of the companies you profile I already know, and it's always fun to hear them describe it versus what I see at their company because of course they're not always same, but that's just human nature. We all do that. And so anyway, I hope you continue doing what you're doing, Lenny, and I'll keep following.
turns.zh: 我觉得这完全没问题。而且，我觉得你也不想吓跑嘉宾。这确实是他们分享自己认为重要内容的平台。我确实觉得很有趣，因为你介绍的很多公司我都认识，听他们描述与我在公司看到的不同总是很有趣，毕竟两者不完全一样，但这就是人性，我们都会这样。总之，Lenny，希望你继续做你正在做的事，我会一直关注的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I appreciate it. And same to you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。非常感谢。你也是。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So with the writing, I think an implication with the way you're describing is basically you're telling people things they don't want to hear but they need to hear. That's the way you think about it, right?
turns.zh: 说到写作，我觉得你描述的方式暗示着你基本上是在告诉人们他们不想听但又必须听的话。这就是你的看法，对吧？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: I do. In fact, I've got some very uncomfortable things to talk about, which I know the more intelligent part of me is like, "Don't bring that up." But also the other side of me is like, "But people need to hear it."
turns.zh: 是的。事实上，我有一些非常令人不舒服的话要说，我知道我更明智的一面会说，“别提这个。”但另一方面又会说，“但人们需要听。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's talk about it if people need to hear it, which I agree. So you've been talking about this concept of product management theater and product leadership theater. Let's get into it. What does that look like? What is the sign that you're in this theater versus doing it the way you should be doing it?
turns.zh: 既然人们需要听，那我们就谈谈吧，我也同意。所以你一直在谈论产品管理剧场和产品领导力剧场这个概念。让我们深入探讨一下。这看起来是什么样的？怎样才能判断自己身处这场“剧场”而不是按照正确的方式行事？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: There is no question that a lot of companies overhired during the pandemic. That was easy to see even while it was going on. And it's not just that they overhired, a lot of them lowered the bar. But at the same time, of course we have a change in the financial world that has really increased the cost of funds. And that's another thing going on simultaneously. And probably one of the biggest things of all, and this is the hardest because it's not happened yet, is the predicted impact of generative AI, right? I don't know if you saw, literally the CEO of NVIDIA the other day was saying don't learn programming. (00:13:34): First of all, I'm not even sure that's good advice, but the fact that the CEO of one of the most amazing companies in the world is saying don't learn programming, that's disruptive. And so at a minimum it creates uncertainty among the leaders in the companies, at a minimum. But honestly, I think there's very real impact. I'm convinced of that. I just don't know the real time horizon. I've got a long history of being overly optimistic. I think things are going to happen sooner than they really do. So I don't know when they'll really happen, but that's a big one. Here's another one that I think is not talked nearly enough about, and that is in a lot of companies, especially outside of Silicon Valley, team size has just gotten out of hand. I go into some companies and honestly I can't believe all the ridiculous roles that they have. And I'll go into that more if you want later, but no question that people realize that smaller teams can often produce more and better results. (00:14:44): How many of your guests have said as much? I've heard it from many of them. It's reducing the size of the organization ironically can get you a lot more in terms of results. So there's this general appreciation that maybe we overdid it here with all of these roles. And of course I'm talking about agile coaches and product owners and product ops and business analysts and all these assistant product manager types. So we'll go into that if you want, but it's gotten out of hand at a lot of companies. And then the one that I really probably shouldn't bring up just because it's become a religious topic almost. I know it's a super sensitive topic for people, but the reality is with remote employees, both velocity and innovation have taken a real hit. Now we can talk about, don't get me wrong, I don't think we're ever going to go back to the days of big companies having almost all co-located teams. (00:15:49): But there is no question, I work with a lot of them, they are all struggling with innovation and velocity. Things go slower and they don't really do that level of innovation that they used to do. And these are big factors, these are macro factors that are going on. And then on top of that, if you get outside of the Silicon Valley bubble, it's even worse because they have been investing at these companies, especially the big companies in all these extra roles. I mentioned agile coaches, but scrum masters and every flavor of project manager you could dream up, they're everywhere and every kind of assistant to product people. I think it's gotten crazy. In fact, I wrote an article a long time ago, something like a decade ago that was very popular at the time called Epic Waste, and I was pointing this out and saying this is crazy. The ironic thing is that the better companies do way more with a lot less. (00:16:55): So anyway, the roles. And then what about all the years that have been going on where they think these big companies think the answer lies in processes, especially things like safe, which outside of the Silicon Valley world is depressingly popular? And even though scrum, a lot of people don't even understand simple processes like scrum and they miss the point. So what's going on in so much of the world is they have so little in the way of outcomes to show for all this cost. And we talked about the sheer number of people becomes a problem and the amount of that cost can be shocking and the amount of waste is basically embarrassing. So it is not a surprise to me that companies are reacting to that. The bigger surprise honestly is it's taken so long for so many companies to realize what is going on. (00:17:51): And bottom line is today I think everybody, especially outside in those big process and role heavy companies, they need to take a hard look at how they build products and how they serve their customers. And they need to look harder at how the best companies do this with so much less proportional spend and so much more real return and really take a fresh look at how to best meet the needs of their customers. That's what transformation is about, is moving to work like that. And the ones that do that well I think are the ones with the best chance to survive.
turns.zh:
毫无疑问，许多公司在疫情期间过度招聘了。即使在疫情期间，这一点也很明显。不仅是招聘过多，很多公司还降低了招聘标准。但与此同时，金融领域的变化也大幅推高了资金成本，这也是同期发生的另一重大事件。最重要的是，人工智能的潜在影响——这可能是最难预测的因素。（00:13:34）：首先，我甚至不确定这是否是明智建议，但全球最杰出公司之一的首席执行官说不要学习编程，这本身就具有颠覆性。至少，这在公司高管中引发了不确定性。说实话，我认为其影响非常真实。我深信这一点，只是不知道具体时间节点。我向来过于乐观，总是低估事情发生的速度。所以我不确定具体时间，但这确实是个重大问题。还有一个几乎未被充分讨论的问题，那就是许多公司——尤其是硅谷以外的公司——团队规模已经失控了。我走访一些公司时，简直不敢相信他们设置的那些荒谬职位。稍后我会详细谈论这个问题，但毫无疑问，人们意识到小团队往往能产出更多、更好的成果。（00:14:44）：有多少嘉宾也这么说过？我听过很多人的看法。讽刺的是，缩减组织规模反而能带来更好的成果。因此，人们普遍意识到我们在这些角色上可能做得过头了。当然，我说的是敏捷教练、产品负责人、产品运营、业务分析师以及各种助理产品经理之类的。如果你们感兴趣，我们可以深入探讨，但很多公司在这方面已经失控了。还有一个我本不该提及的话题，因为它几乎成了一个宗教般的信仰。我知道这对人们来说是个敏感话题，但现实是，远程员工的效率和创新能力都受到了严重影响。别误会，我们可以讨论，但我认为大公司不可能再回到几乎全员集中办公的时代了。（00:15:49）：但毫无疑问，我与许多大公司合作过，他们都在为创新和效率苦苦挣扎。进展缓慢，创新水平远不及从前。这些都是宏观层面的重大因素。更糟糕的是，如果你离开硅谷泡沫，情况会更糟，因为这些大公司，尤其是那些大公司，过度投资于这些额外角色。我提到了敏捷教练，但还有Scrum主管和各种你能想象到的项目经理，他们无处不在，充当产品团队的各种助手。我认为这已经失控了。事实上，十多年前我写过一篇当时很受欢迎的文章，叫《史诗级浪费》，我就指出过这个问题，称其疯狂至极。讽刺的是，更优秀的公司用更少的资源就能做得更多。（00:16:55）：总之，职位设置问题。那么在过去这些年里，人们认为这些大公司认为
答案在于流程，尤其是像安全这类东西，在硅谷之外的世界里却令人沮丧地普及？即便像Scrum这样的敏捷框架，许多人甚至连最基础的流程都理解不透彻，完全误解了其核心要义。全球范围内，太多企业在投入巨资却收效甚微。人员规模过大已成顽疾，成本规模令人震惊，浪费程度简直令人尴尬。因此，企业对此做出调整并不意外。但更令人惊讶的是，许多公司花了这么久才意识到问题的严重性。（00:17:51）归根结底，我认为当下所有企业——尤其是那些流程繁琐、角色分工过度复杂的大型公司——都必须深刻反思产品开发与客户服务的本质。它们需要仔细研究顶尖企业是如何以更低的成本投入、更高的实际回报率来满足客户需求的，并重新审视如何最有效地满足客户需求。这才是转型真正的意义所在——向这样的工作模式转型。而那些能成功实现这一转型的企业，才最有可能在未来立足。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's just this broader trend of people just really dislike PMs in a lot of places. There's this just trend of I don't want PMs at my company, I don't want PMs at my startup. For a long time, we're going to have no PMs. It's like this general idea, and I think you're saying a lot of this comes from many people who were hired as product managers that are not good at the job and people's experience with PMs is those sorts of people.
turns.zh: 我认为，在很多地方，人们确实对产品经理普遍反感。这是一种趋势——比如“我不想让公司有产品经理”、“我不想让创业公司有产品经理”。很长一段时间内，我们可能都不会再有产品经理了。这种观念很普遍，我觉得你提到的情况大多源于许多被聘为产品经理却不胜任工作的人，以及人们对产品经理的负面体验。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: I think it's a different really answer. And I haven't gone into this, but you probably. Those examples, with very few exceptions, and I hear it all the time, almost every day, what you're describing, they're feature teams. And the truth is, and I've been saying this for a long time, the truth is they don't need PMs in a feature team. They don't because it's a project management role, Lenny, and they already have plenty of people who can cover that. And furthermore, a lot of times the engineers or the designers say, "We'd rather do it ourselves than deal with this person that's got this complex and trying to be the boss of everybody and they really don't contribute anything." So that's what's really going on in my view. They are either a delivery team or a feature team, usually a feature team in this model. (00:19:49): And I don't blame those people for not finding value in the product manager. They are just not bringing that value. They do bring a little value, in fairness, but, and this is very brutal, but they're dramatically overpaid for the value they provide. Now on the other hand, in a real product team, that's a very different job and I don't see that. In fact, I consider that complaint you're raising as the biggest clue that they're probably our feature team. And then I'll go ask them how they're working and what that person... And then of course the first thing I ask the product manager is how do you define your job? And I bet you've heard a hundred variations of the mealy mouth, squishy, I facilitate this and I do some communication and I herd the cats and I'm listening to that going, man, I would not want to try to defend that job to the CEO.
turns.zh: 我认为这其实是个误区。虽然我没深入探讨过，但你可能已经注意到了。那些例子，除了极少数情况外，我每天都能听到你所描述的情况——这些都是功能团队。说实话，我长期以来一直强调，功能团队根本不需要产品经理。原因在于，产品经理本质上是项目管理角色，而功能团队中已经有足够多的人能胜任这个角色。此外，工程师或设计师经常说：“我们宁愿自己做，也不愿和这个复杂的人打交道，他总想当老大却毫无贡献。”在我看来，问题就在于他们要么是交付团队，要么是功能团队，在这种模式下通常是功能团队。（00:19:49）我不怪那些人觉得产品经理没价值——他们确实没提供价值。说句难听的，他们提供的价值微乎其微。现在说另一方面，真正的产品团队的工作完全不同，我从未见过这样的团队。事实上，我认为你提到的这些抱怨恰恰是最明显的迹象，表明他们很可能是功能团队。然后我会去问他们如何开展工作，问那个产品经理……当然，我首先会问产品经理如何定义自己的工作职责。我敢打赌，你肯定听过无数种含糊其辞、模棱两可的回答，比如“我负责协调沟通、管好团队、倾听需求”之类的。听了这些，我只能想，天哪，我可不想向CEO解释这种工作内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you talk about teams and product teams a lot. I imagine people still aren't 100% sure of exactly what you mean when you say that. So let's spend a little time on just what does it look like when you're on a feature team, feature factory versus an empowered product team?
turns.zh: 我知道你经常谈论团队和产品团队。我猜人们对你的定义还是不太清楚。所以我们花点时间详细讲讲功能团队、功能工厂和授权型产品团队的区别吧？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Well, there's a lot of clues for sure. Some of the easiest is on a feature team, you're basically given a roadmap of output. That's the key, is output. In other words, their features are projects that usually it could have come from an executive, could have come from a big pocket customer, could have come from wherever. But it's a bunch of features and literally you're being asked to design, build, test, deploy that feature. You're usually given dates and timeframes as well, but that's a feature team. You deliver. And don't get me wrong, that's still work, but that's output. It is a lot easier to deliver output than it is to deliver outcomes. And a product team, an empowered product team, instead of being given that roadmap of features, they're given problems to solve. Now they're customer problems or they're business problems or both, but they're given a problem to solve. (00:21:57): Usually one or two a quarter on top of of course the keep the lights on kind of work that everybody does, but they're given hard problems to solve and the measure is not ship the thing. The measure is it solves the problem. And that's why really the biggest difference between a strong product company and the rest is strong product companies understand it's all about outcomes. You just don't get points for shipping, you get points for delivering the value. A lot of the CEOs and CFOs I talk to, they resonate best when I frame it as it's about time to money more than time to market. We know how to do time to market. If you insist on time to market, we know how to do that. The techniques are well-known. The harder part is time to money and I know that's what they care about and that's harder and that's what a product team really does. (00:22:51): It's only when you sign up for an outcome that you have the needs for a product manager. I would say in the Silicon Valley sense, that's when you need a product manager. Because if you've been asked to solve these problems, that means you have to come up with a solution that's not only usable and feasible, which is what a feature team does, but is also valuable and viable. And that means you need a different set of skills that your engineers and your designers almost never have. That's not a knock on them. Those are very different skillsets. So now you need this person who understands the customers and understands the business deeply. That's where the product manager role came from. That's what they still at a good product company are responsible for. So that's a very different job. It's also if you have a person playing that kind of product manager, it is very unlikely they've got time on their hands to get in the face of the designer and start wire framing for them or start irritating the developers. They've got their own work to do.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实有很多线索。最明显的一个例子是，在功能团队中，你基本上会得到一个输出的路线图。这才是关键所在——输出。换句话说，他们的功能是项目，这些项目可能来自高管，可能来自大客户，可能来自其他任何地方。但这是一堆功能，你被要求设计、构建、测试并部署这些功能。通常还会给你设定日期和时间框架，但这就是功能团队的工作模式。你需要交付成果。别误会，这确实是工作，但这只是输出。相比之下，交付成果要比交付结果容易得多。而产品团队，一个有权限的产品团队，不是被赋予功能路线图，而是被赋予需要解决的问题。这些可能是客户问题、商业问题，也可能是两者兼有，但他们被赋予一个需要解决的问题。（00:21:57）：通常每个季度有一两个项目，此外还有每个人都要做的日常维护工作，但他们被赋予难题去解决。衡量标准不是交付产品，而是解决问题。正因如此，真正强大的产品公司与其他公司的最大区别在于，强大的产品公司深知一切都关乎结果。你不会因为交付产品而获得加分，而是因为交付价值而获得加分。我与许多首席执行官和首席财务官交流时，当我把这件事框定为关注时间换取金钱而非时间换取市场时，他们最容易产生共鸣。我们知道如何做到时间换取市场。如果你执着于时间换取市场，我们也知道怎么做。这些技巧是众所周知的。更难的是时间换取金钱，而我知道这才是他们真正关心的——这更难，这才是产品团队真正要做的。（00:22:51）：只有当你致力于一个结果时，你才需要产品经理。从硅谷的角度来看，这就是你需要产品经理的时候。因为如果你被要求解决这些问题，这意味着你必须提出一个不仅可用且可行的解决方案（这是功能团队的工作），还要具有价值和可行性。这意味着你需要一套不同的技能，而你的工程师和设计师几乎从不具备这些技能。这不是对他们的贬低，只是技能组合截然不同。所以现在你需要这个人，他们要深刻理解客户和业务。这就是产品经理角色的由来。这也是在优秀的产品公司里，产品经理仍然负责的工作。所以这是一份截然不同的工作。即使有产品经理在做产品经理的工作，很可能他们也没有时间去指导设计师或去烦扰开发者。他们自己也有工作要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is essentially the theater you're describing, that people that aren't real product managers doing product management activities, can you just talk about what that looks like?
turns.zh: 而这基本上就是你所描述的现状，即那些不是真正的产品经理却在做产品管理工作的人，你能否谈谈这是什么样子的？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: The biggest example of that is that they carry this title product manager because the whole world largely, thanks to you, knows it's cool, but they're not doing any of the role and they don't have any of the skills. Now of course, what really bothers me is it's not that hard if they are motivated. It's not that hard for them to develop the skills, and that's what I talk to people about. You can raise your game so that you actually can contribute at this level. That's what you should do for your own career, but by the way, and not accidentally, that's what your company needs you to do.
turns.zh: 其中最典型的例子就是，他们挂着“产品经理”的头衔，却对产品经理的核心职责一无所知。全世界之所以普遍认为产品经理是个酷炫的职位，多亏了你们的宣传，但这些人既不履行产品经理的职责，也不具备相关技能。当然，最让我困扰的是——只要他们有上进心，这一切其实并不难。培养这些技能并不难，这也是我经常跟大家强调的——只要你能提升自己的能力，就能真正胜任产品经理的角色。这不仅对你的职业发展至关重要，更重要的是，这正是你的公司所需要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And for people that are listening to this wondering, what are these skills that I need to build to be a real product manager? I think you often say it's mostly focused on value and viability, and that's where a lot of this-
turns.zh: 可能有些听众会问：要成为真正的产品经理，到底需要掌握哪些技能？我认为核心在于价值创造和商业可行性，而这正是产品经理工作的核心——

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Value and viability is what you are responsible for as a product manager, just like an engineer is responsible for feasibility, it has to be a solution that can be built and delivered. But a product manager is responsible for value and viability. Another way I like to frame this is on a real empowered product team, product manager is a creator, not a facilitator. I always cringe when somebody tells me, oh, my job is to say why? And I'm like, "Well, what do you do for the rest of the week besides the 10 minutes it takes you to say why?" It's ridiculous. People think that. But you know what? On a feature team, when you're scrounging around for some justification of your job, it's not that big a surprise. But no, the why actually comes from the product strategy anyway. You don't even do the why. (00:25:45): A product manager is a creator and so there's this side-by-side creation with design and engineering to come up with these solutions. Now, in order to do your job and represent value and viability, there are some real skills that are involved. First of all, you have to really become an expert on your users and customers. I know that I was not allowed to take the product manager role until I had visited 30 customers in person, 15 in the US, 15 in Europe. That was just the person who was coaching me. That was their rule. And all I know is those 30 customers changed my life because I thought I knew our customers and I really didn't. Another is you're supposed to be the expert on the data. How is our product being used? How is that usage changing over time? How is it being purchased? So that's big. Another big one is you are the person on the team that represents the compliance issues, the sales issues, the marketing issues, the financial cost issues, the monetization issues, go to market in general. (00:26:51): This is all legal constraints. This is all the product manager. Just think if you don't have this person on the team and you want to empower this team to make decisions, what are you going to do? You're just going to make it up? Or what they usually do is they call meetings with 20 stakeholders all in a room to try to decide these things, and now you've reverted to design by committee. So no, the product manager needs to bring this knowledge. They also need to bring deep understanding of the market. So when I describe these things to a typical product owner, they're like, "We're on different planets." What they learned in a CSPO or a PSPO class was how to manage a backlog in Jira, which to me is very analogous to learning how to operate Google Docs. Of course, that's not the job. That's something we do every day, but it's not the job just any more than... (00:27:50): Developers are in Jira every day. Does that mean that's their job? Of course not. Their job is to build. So this is what a product manager contributes. And really the distinction, if you want to think about it on a spectrum, a product owner is one extreme. And honestly, that is a role in a delivery process. That has no business being a dedicated person, really doesn't. And most teams I know, the senior engineer could do it better anyway. Second on the other side of the spectrum is what we're talking about, an empowered product manager. And then a feature team product manager is somewhere in between there. They do more than administer the backlog. They do a lot of project management. And don't get me wrong, project management is important, but it is not product management. And furthermore, in almost every company I see with feature team product managers, they have a boatload of project managers anyway. (00:28:51): So you could hear there's some exasperation in my voice because I feel like this has been quite clear for a long time, but most companies are deaf to this. They don't care. And I have theories about why, but that's kind of depressing. But for whatever reason, I feel like now I'm raising the volume because people are now seeing this the hard way because a lot of companies are cutting and these are easily among the most vulnerable people in a company.
turns.zh:
价值与可行性是产品经理的职责所在，正如工程师负责产品的可行性一样，产品经理必须确保提出的解决方案既可落地又能实现商业价值。但产品经理的核心职责在于创造价值与验证可行性。我更愿意用另一种方式来阐释这一点——在真正赋权的产品团队中，产品经理是创作者，而非协调者。每当有人跟我说"我的工作就是说服别人"时，我都会感到不屑，"那你一周剩下的时间除了花10分钟说服别人之外还做了什么？"这简直可笑。人们总有这种误解。但当你身处一个功能团队，绞尽脑汁为自己的工作寻找合理性时，这种困境其实并不意外。然而，产品的真正价值和可行性并非源自个人推理——而是基于产品战略的顶层设计。产品经理无需亲自完成这项工作。

（00:25:45）产品经理是创作者，与设计和工程团队并肩协作，共同构思解决方案。要履行职责并体现价值与可行性，需具备多项核心技能。首先，你必须成为用户与客户的深度专家。我记得在担任产品经理之前，必须亲自拜访30位客户——其中15位在美国，15位在欧洲。这是指导我的导师设定的门槛。其次，数据专家是必备角色。产品如何被使用？使用行为如何随时间演变？购买路径如何？这些关键数据都需要深入解析。再者，产品经理还需统筹合规、销售、营销、成本控制与变现等全局事务。（00:26:51）这些都是法律层面的硬性要求。这些职责都应由产品经理承担。若团队中缺乏此类专员，决策权下放只会导致集体决策的混乱局面。

（00:27:50）开发者日常使用Jira管理Backlog，但这绝非产品经理的核心职责。多数产品负责人仅停留在CSPO或PSPO课程中学习的"Backlog管理"层面——这与实际工作相去甚远。真正的产品经理需要深厚的市场洞察力。这让我想起一个典型产品负责人的反应："我们完全不在同一个维度上。"他们所熟练的JiraBacklog管理与产品经理的职责根本不可同日而语。

（00:28:20）功能团队中的产品经理则处于两者之间。他们不仅管理Backlog，还承担项目管理重任。项目管理固然重要，但绝非产品管理的全部内涵。以我观察到的功能团队产品经理为例，多数情况下他们的职责可以由高级工程师更好地完成。
反正项目经理多得是。（00:28:51）：所以你能听出我语气里有些不满，因为我觉得这一点很久以前就已经很明显了，但大多数公司对此充耳不闻。他们根本不在乎。我对原因有自己的看法，但这有点令人沮丧。不过不管怎样，我觉得现在我得把声音调大，因为很多人现在正吃苦头，因为很多公司都在裁员，而这些人往往是公司里最脆弱的群体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me actually read a quote from you where you talk about this exact point. You wrote, "I have been warning for several years that delivery team, product owners and feature team product managers are likely to be facing a reckoning as companies realize that these roles are not what they thought they were. From what I can tell, that reckoning has begun and I'm expecting GenAI will only compound this."
turns.zh: 让我来读一读你提到这一观点的引述部分。你写道："我多年来一直警告，随着公司意识到交付团队、产品负责人和特性团队产品经理的角色并非他们想象中的那样，这些角色很可能面临重大调整。从目前情况看，这种调整已经开始，我预计GenAI只会让情况雪上加霜。"

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: That's the pessimistic version of the world. Either I might be overreacting. Might be. I'm not really known for being alarmist, but maybe. It's possible. I hope so, but I doubt it. I think these trends are real. Now, does that mean people are... It's hopeless? They should all start retraining to be, I don't know what, housing construction, something that GenAI won't replace maybe? No. I think what really this does is you need to raise your skills. Enough with the silly facades of delivery teams and feature teams. You should raise your skills. And a lot of product managers, they reach out and they're like, "I know I'm in a feature team and I don't like it." I often use the phrase they're trapped in a feature team and they're like, "This isn't what I signed up for. The New York Times article about product management wasn't this. This was different." And they're like, "What should I do? Should I just leave my company and go to one of these other companies?" (00:31:01): And I try to explain that they actually have a lot more agency than they realize. There is a lot an individual contributor... Of course, there's way more than a product leader could do. And that's the biggest shame in all this, is they're not doing this. Most product leaders are not doing this 'cause they of course have a lot of agency, a lot of ability to change a company. But an individual can do it as well. They can raise their game. They can literally do a self-assessment and raise the skills from a product owner or a feature team product manager to a real product manager. At a minimum, I tell people, and I've seen this countless times, at a minimum, your company will appreciate it and probably promote you because you will be one of the few that actually understands these things. Hopefully even more than that, they'll say, hey, why don't we try running a set of teams this way and see how we do? So it can happen from the ground up too.
turns.zh: 这就是对世界的悲观看法。或许我反应过度了。有可能吧。我向来不以危言耸听著称，但也许有这种可能。我希望情况并非如此，但恐怕事实如此。我认为这些趋势是真实存在的。那么，这是否意味着人们……就此无望了？他们应该全部开始重新培训，去从事什么行业？比如住房建设之类的领域，也许GenAI不会取代这些行业？不。我认为真正需要做的是提升自己的技能。别再装模作样地玩什么交付团队和特性团队的游戏了。你应该提升自己的技能。很多产品经理会抱怨："我知道自己在特性团队里，但我不喜欢这种工作。"我常说他们被困在特性团队里，就像他们会说："这不是我当初签约要做的。《纽约时报》关于产品管理的文章不是这样描述的。"然后他们会问："我该怎么办？是该离开公司去其他公司吗？"（00:31:01）我试图向他们解释，他们实际上比自己意识到的拥有更多自主权。个体贡献者……当然，产品负责人的能力远超产品经理。但这才是最令人遗憾的地方——他们没有行动起来。大多数产品负责人没有行动起来，因为他们显然拥有更强的自主权和改变公司的能力。但个人也可以做到。他们可以提升自己的能力，可以进行自我评估，将产品负责人的技能或特性团队产品经理的技能提升到真正的产品经理水平。至少，我告诉人们——而且我见过无数这样的例子——至少你的公司会欣赏你的努力，可能还会提拔你，因为你将成为为数不多真正理解这些事物的人之一。希望更多公司会因此改变策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine many people are wondering, how do I do this? I know you've written books, I guess there's courses, there's all kinds of things. If you could give people a couple tips of how to get better at this and what skills to focus on, what's a quick piece of advice you could share there?
turns.zh: 我能想象很多人都在想，如何做到这一点？我知道你写过书，应该有相关课程之类的。如果你能给人们一些提升技能的建议，哪些技能值得关注，你能分享些快速入门的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Well, this is maybe the most frustrating thing to me of all. And in fact, I should have answered when you asked me what motivated me to get spicy, what pushed me over the edge. Maybe I was in a bad mood that day, I don't know. But it was this article that made the rounds online by probably the biggest certification institution for product managers. And they had this big article saying, "This is what a product manager does." And it was a big graphic, and I'm looking at it and I was thinking, I cannot believe they said this out loud. This is 100% project manager, 100%. They didn't even pretend to put a little of the product, which most people of course are more creative than that. They bend over a little bit to make it look like a product manager, but not even close. (00:33:11): And what I realized is what's so frustrating here is you have all these people that realize things aren't good yet most places they turn are just propagating that same model. So these certifications, which in my opinion are bogus, but most people don't know. And just imagine you're a brand new product manager. You look online probably what, 90% of the content out there is from the feature team world or worst. And so unless they get really lucky or they happen to be really lucky and have a manager that is guiding them in a good direction, it just propagates. And you see this all over, articles, books, conference speakers, and a lot of times I can't even bear to watch. And it's not like there aren't great people out there who can speak. It's just that proportionally they're in the minority. So it's not as easy as it should be. Like you're saying, why can't people just go and learn? (00:34:14): They can if they're lucky enough to know where to go. Obviously I'm biased. You're biased too. We're biased on this, but people need to take more control of their career and really use their judgment, try to figure out what do you want to be if you want to be in the product world? What do you want to be? What kind of a product manager do you want to be? And if you want to stay, fine, but if you want to do this, then there are good resources for sure. There are good resources out there. And of course, I'm hoping more and more people do that.
turns.zh: 嗯，这或许是我最感到沮丧的一件事了。事实上，当你问我是什么促使我选择做产品经理，什么让我下定决心时，我本该给出一个更完整的答案的。也许那天我心情不佳，我也不清楚。但真正让我气愤的，是那篇由国内最大的产品经理认证机构在网上疯传的文章。他们在一篇大型图文内容里声称：“这就是产品经理的工作！” 配图是一张大图，我看着它时简直不敢相信他们会公然说出这种话。这完全就是项目经理的职责啊，百分之百！他们甚至没有稍作掩饰，让它看起来像产品经理的工作。（00:33:11）我意识到，最令人沮丧的是，大多数人意识到现状不佳，却发现周围大多数机构都在宣扬同样的模式。这些认证在我看来就是骗局，但大多数人并不知情。想象一下，如果你是一个初出茅庐的产品经理。你在网上看到的内容，90%可能来自功能团队领域，甚至更糟糕。除非你运气极好，或者恰好遇到了能给你正确引导的经理，否则这种错误观念就会不断传播。你随处可见这样的内容——文章、书籍、会议演讲者——很多时候我甚至不忍心看下去。并不是说没有优秀的人能分享正确的见解，而是相较而言，他们只是少数派。所以这并不像应该的那样容易。就像你说的，为什么人们不能去学习呢？（00:34:14）如果他们足够幸运能找到正确的资源，那当然可以。我也有偏见。你也有偏见。我们在这件事上都有偏见，但人们需要更多地掌控自己的职业生涯，运用自己的判断力，去思考如果你想在产品领域发展，你想成为什么样的人？你想成为什么样的产品经理？如果你想留在现有岗位，那没问题，但如果你想有所作为，那肯定有优质的资源可供利用。当然，我希望越来越多的人能这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such a powerful insight you just shared, that most of the content you find online about product management is, I think you called it 90%, or it's just from companies that are not doing it the right way, feature teams is the way you described it. Can you talk a bit more about that? Why is that the case? Why don't we hear more from great companies?
turns.zh: 我觉得你刚刚分享的见解非常深刻，你说在网上找到的大多数产品管理相关内容，可能是90%来自那些做得不对的公司，或者是功能团队的视角。你能再多谈谈这个吗？为什么会这样？为什么我们听不到更多来自优秀公司的声音？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: In fact, one of the most frustrating things for me is community. One of the things that's great about community... You have one of the biggest communities today, but there's a lot of these communities out there in the product world, product sub communities. And the one I love about them is pretty much everybody you meet genuinely wants to help. Really everybody. The problem is somebody posts a question, happens many times every day, and the majority of the well-meaning people jump in with what they learn at their crappy company. And I'm looking at that and the person is, oh, thank you very much, now I know what to do. And I'm going, "Oh no, there goes another one." It becomes self-propagating. And what are you going to do? Is somebody going to try to police these boards, thousands and thousands of them, like a Lenny endorsed person or a Marty endorsed person? I don't want to do that. You probably don't want to do that.
turns.zh: 事实上，最让我感到沮丧的事情之一就是社区。社区的优点之一……你现在所处的社区规模庞大，但产品领域里还有无数类似的子社区。我最欣赏它们的地方在于，几乎每个你遇到的人都真心想提供帮助。真的，每个人都是如此。但问题是，当有人提出问题时——这种情况每天都会发生——大多数好心的人会把自己在糟糕公司学到的东西硬塞给别人。看到这种情况，我会想，"哦，太感谢你了，现在我知道该怎么做了。"但我心里却在说："天哪，又来一个。"这种情况会自我循环。你能怎么办？难道要派个像Lenny或Marty这样的人去监管这些数以千计的社区吗？我可不想这么做。你大概也不想这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: It's a recipe for disaster. So there are so many reasons it propagates. Most of the books I see, I'm asked to review a lot of the books. I love it when it's an exception and it's like, wow, that's a good book. Teresa Torres's book, Continuous Discovery Habits, good book. Try to get everybody to read that. But that's the exception. And most of the time people are earnestly describing what they learn, not really what good companies do. So it's very difficult because these are not bad people. They're well-meaning.
turns.zh: 这简直就是个灾难。这种情况之所以会蔓延，有很多原因。我看过的绝大多数书籍，我都被要求写书评。偶尔遇到一本例外的好书，比如特蕾莎·托雷斯的《持续探索习惯》，我会大力推荐。但这种情况毕竟是少数。大多数时候，人们都在真诚地分享自己的经验，而不是讲述优秀公司的做法。这真的很让人头疼，因为这些人本身并不坏，他们都是善意的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any advice for somebody asking questions, getting answers, and having a sense of, should I listen to these people?
turns.zh: 对于那些提问、得到答案，却又不知道该不该听信这些人的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: It's very much this exists in the whole world, right? Buyer beware. You have to use your judgment. You have to think. Probably the most important skill for product people, and I know this sounds awful, but is really learning how to think critically. And that involves literally evaluating. I know I talk to people all the time when I help them for their interviewing. I say, "Look, the most important thing, you need to do some research on the manager that will be your direct manager. Do some background research. Go look at where they worked. It's all on LinkedIn. Check out those companies, check out that product. Make sure you are prepared there because that's what really matters. Not so much the company, but who's going to coach you." So there's a lot that people can do to prepare themselves, arm themselves, take more ownership of their career.
turns.zh: 这种情况在全世界都存在，对吧？买家需谨慎。你得用自己的判断力。你得思考。对我来说，产品经理最重要的技能——虽然这听起来很糟糕——就是学会如何批判性思考。这就需要实实在在地评估。我在帮助别人准备面试时经常说："看，最重要的是，你得对你的直属经理做些背景调查。去看看他们曾在哪家公司工作过。这些信息都在领英上。去看看那些公司，了解他们的产品。确保你对这些做好准备，因为这才是关键所在。不是公司本身，而是谁会指导你。"所以人们可以通过很多方式来提升自己，增强自我主导能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting, I'm sure you'll run into this and I'll just share something that I thought of. So while I was at Airbnb, I was reading your stuff and I was like, "Who works like this? He's talking about all these companies that are working in this strange way of just being given a roadmap." I'm like, "No way. This is not a thing. What is he writing about?" And it's because I was working at a company that does things well, and I know you disagree with where things have gotten. But anyway, so I imagine many people listening to this are like, I don't believe this is how a lot of companies work. What are you talking about? And then I also imagine there's a large percentage of people that work at a feature factory and they're just like, no, it's fine. It's not actually the way you're describing. So I bet this is quite frustrating for you.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我相信你也会遇到这种情况，我只想分享一下我的想法。在Airbnb工作期间，我读了你的文章，心想："谁会这样工作？他讲的那些公司都是按照某种奇怪的模式运作的，直接给他们一份路线图就行了。"我简直不敢相信。这根本不是现实。他在写什么鬼东西？而这正是因为我在一家做事规范的公司工作过，我知道你对现状的不满。但不管怎样，我能想象很多听众会说："我不相信很多公司都是这样运作的。你在说什么呢？"我敢打赌，还有很大一部分在功能工厂工作的人会说："不，没关系。情况并非你所描述的那样。"所以我敢说这对你来说一定很令人沮丧。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Yeah, I've experienced that 'cause I spent most of my career in that same bubble, and I was so surprised to find that people didn't work the way we did. I remember when it was too, because I was a developer at the time for developer tools, and I was building tools assuming that people were building like we built. And then I was sent out, I remember because one of the most eye-opening visits was my very first visit to Walmart's headquarters. And they were doing things so differently. They had just very different way of working, very different equipment, just everything. And it was a wake-up call. It was like, you know what? I'm living in a bubble. Silicon Valley is not like most of the world here. And of course I realized that why not? Why don't companies in Arkansas and India and everywhere else have the access to the same methods and tools and techniques? And so that became the inspiration for Silicon Valley Product Group, was to spread those things. (00:39:56): But I've had that exact conversation. I remember as you're saying it, the first time Shreyas Doshi told me the same thing. He was asking me, 'cause he had known me, and I'm like, "I know you write about this stuff, but I really can't believe people are doing this." And I'm like, "Shreyas, I wish it wasn't true." But he doesn't doubt it today.
turns.zh: 是的，我有过这样的经历，因为我的职业生涯大部分时间都处于同样的「泡沫」之中。当我发现其他人的工作方式与我们截然不同时，真是大吃一惊。我记得当时的情景——我当时是开发工具的开发者，总以为别人和我们一样开发产品。后来我被派出去访问，记得最震撼的一次是第一次去沃尔玛总部。他们做事的方式完全不同，设备、流程等等都与我们天差地别。这让我如梦初醒，意识到自己一直生活在一个封闭的圈子里。硅谷毕竟不是世界其他地方的典型代表。当然，我也意识到为什么不呢？为什么阿肯色州、印度等地的公司就不能获得同样的方法、工具和技术呢？于是这成了我创立硅谷产品集团的灵感源泉——就是要把这些理念传播出去。（00:39:56）：但我也曾有过完全相同的对话。记得你说这话时，施雷亚斯·多希第一次对我说了同样的话。他问我：“你写过相关内容，但我真不敢相信人们会这样做。”我回答：“施雷亚斯，我也希望这不是真的。”但他现在对此深信不疑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, 'cause he is doing a lot of that work now too. I'm curious if it's okay for people to be on a feature team and just stick with it and be happy. There's actually this LinkedIn post today by this PM, [inaudible 00:40:31] Ben Erez who talks about how if there's a B2B sales driven company, maybe it's okay for it to be feature factory where people know exactly what you need to build. You build these things, it's fine. We don't need you to inform our outcomes. Thoughts on that? Is it ever okay to just be like, it's fine?
turns.zh: 是啊，因为他现在也在做很多这类工作。我很好奇，人们是否能在一个特性团队中安心待着并乐在其中。今天LinkedIn上有个产品经理本·埃雷兹的帖子，他提到如果是一家B2B销售驱动型公司，也许可以采用“特性工厂”的模式，让人们清楚知道需要构建什么。只要能完成这些任务就行，不需要告知最终结果。对此你怎么看？就这样安于现状真的没问题吗？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Well, my first answer is this is not an accident why most B2B software is such crap. It is horrible. And of course, the ones that really stand out, they usually are not this way. So sales driven product, don't get me wrong. There's companies like Oracle that are massively valuable, driven with sales driven product, but do you really want to be Oracle or do you want to be SAP? Does anybody like those products out there? I don't know. I'm not sure I've ever met anybody that didn't hate those products. So no, I'd say that's just bad product. Now, I would argue that some of my favorite examples... In fact, in the new book we highlighted a classic sales driven financial services company moving to the product model and how it dramatically improved things for the sales organization. (00:41:48): So there's a bigger reason I think so many sales driven companies exist, is that most of the time in those companies, the CEOs are not product people and that's why they run that way. And until and unless the CEO decides this is not very good, usually because some good product company comes along and takes away their customers, that's probably not going to change.
turns.zh: 嗯，我首先要说的是，大多数B2B软件之所以如此糟糕，这绝非偶然。它们实在太烂了。当然，真正出类拔萃的公司通常不走这条路。所以说销售驱动型产品，我没别的意思。像甲骨文这样价值数十亿美元的公司，其产品就是以销售为导向的，但你真的想成为甲骨文吗？还是想成为SAP？市场上有人喜欢这些产品吗？我不知道。我从未遇到过不讨厌这些产品的人。所以不，我认为那就是糟糕的产品。现在，我要说我最喜欢的例子之一……事实上，新书中我们重点介绍了一家典型的销售驱动型金融服务公司转向产品模式后，如何极大地提升了销售团队的效率。（00:41:48）：所以我认为许多销售驱动型公司存在的更深层原因，是这些公司的CEO大多不是产品出身，这就是他们坚持这种管理模式的原因。除非CEO意识到这种模式弊端重重——通常是因为某家优秀的产品公司抢走他们的客户——否则这种情况很难改变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So your feedback there essentially is sure you can operate this way. You're not actually going to build a great product and long term you're going to run into competition [inaudible 00:42:21]?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以你的观点基本上是说，当然你可以这样运作。但你最终不会打造出伟大的产品，长期来看还会面临竞争（[inaudible 00:42:21]）？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: The other thing I'd argue, Lenny, is an empowered product team can do everything a feature team can do and more. And once in a while I do hear somebody say, why isn't it good enough to be a feature team? How do you answer that really? To me, it is like, why are you in this business? Do you really not care what your customers think about your product? Seriously? I know I would never hire you if I had any say because that's one of the first things we want. We want people to genuinely care about our customers and about our business and making lives better for them. So I don't have a lot of sympathy for those people. I do know that there's plenty of resources for them, so they're fine. It's the people that really want to do better than that.
turns.zh: 莱尼，我想说的是，赋权型产品团队能够胜任任何特性团队的职责，甚至超越其范畴。有时我确实听到有人问：为什么特性团队的标准不够高？对此你怎么回应呢？对我来说，这就好比在问——你为什么选择从事这份工作？你真的不在乎客户对你的产品有何看法吗？说真的？要是我有决定权，我绝不会雇用这种人。因为这是我们最看重的东西之一——我们希望团队成员真心关心客户，关注业务发展，为用户创造更美好的生活。所以我对这种人实在没多少同情心。但我知道，市场上有很多资源能满足他们的需求，所以他们也无伤大雅。真正渴望超越现有标准的人才是值得关注的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Reminds me of something your colleague Christian said on our podcast episode of how lucky are we to get to solve people's problems and help them?
turns.zh: 这让我想起你同事克里斯蒂安在我们播客节目中说过的话——我们能有机会解决人们的问题、帮助他们，这是多么幸运的事啊！

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Christian is a living example of what we're talking about. Absolutely. He lives for these opportunities.
turns.zh: 克里斯蒂安就是我们所谈论的典型例子。绝对的。他为这样的机会而生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Vanta. When it comes to ensuring your company has top-notch security practices, things get complicated fast. Now you can assess risk, secure the trust of your customers and automate compliance for SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA and more with a single platform, Vanta. Vanta's market leading trust management platform helps you continuously monitor compliance alongside reporting and tracking risks. Plus you can save hours by completing security questionnaires with Vanta AI. Join thousands of global companies that use Vanta to automate evidence collection, unify risk management, and streamline security reviews. Get $1,000 off Vanta when you go to vanta.com/lenny. That's V-A-N-T-A.com/lenny. (00:44:22): I want to touch on something. So I interviewed the CTO of Meta, and you made this really interesting point. So when I think of Meta/Facebook, I always imagine them as a very bottom-up culture. People on teams build experiments, run things. There's not a lot of do this, do that, but the way that he framed it is it's actually very top-down at Meta. Zuck and the execs come up with here's what we're working on, here's our strategy, here's our big bets. And so he sees it actually as a much more top-down than a bottom-up team, but it seems it comes across as bottom-up, I guess. I know there's a difference between bottom-up versus top-down versus featured factory and empowered product team. But I guess thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 本期节目由Vanta赞助。谈到确保公司拥有一流的安全实践时，事情往往会变得复杂。现在，您可以通过单一平台Vanta评估风险、赢得客户信任，并实现SOC 2、ISO 27001、HIPAA等标准的合规自动化。Vanta的市场领先信任管理平台帮助您持续监控合规情况，同时进行风险报告和追踪。此外，您还可以通过Vanta AI完成安全问卷调查，从而节省数小时时间。数千家全球公司使用Vanta实现证据收集自动化、统一风险管理并简化安全审核流程。访问vanta.com/lenny即可获得1,000美元优惠。（00:44:22）：我想谈谈这个问题。之前我采访了Meta的CTO，你提出了一个很有趣的观点。我一想到Meta/Facebook，总会觉得他们是一种自下而上的文化。团队成员会开发实验项目、自主运作。没有太多命令式的指令，但他描述的实际情况是，Meta实际上是一种自上而下的管理模式。扎克伯格和高管们会提出我们的工作方向、战略重点和重大押注。因此，他认为这实际上更偏向自上而下而非自下而上的团队，但看起来又像是自下而上的。我知道自下而上、自上而下、特性团队和赋权型产品团队之间存在差异。但对此你有什么看法呢？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: So first of all, I would argue what he described is exactly what I see in good product companies, exactly. But we don't frame it as top-down. Top-down is really means something very different. In fact, handing a team a roadmap of features, that's very top-down. Another very common misunderstanding, which comes, again, a lot of the agile coaches, they have misguided so many organizations, but product teams don't do product strategy. Product leaders do product strategy. They need to do the product strategy. And look, I'm not the biggest fan of Meta, but Zuck is very good at product, very good. That's the problem in the world. He's so good at it. But that is the job, is to make these strategic decisions, the focus decisions, the bets you're going to place. But then in a good organization, you give those bets to the teams and you really do give them latitude to figure it out. (00:46:08): And honestly, it's been a while since I worked with Facebook at the time, but they had very good teams, very good product teams, serious cross-functional, serious engineers, serious product managers and designers, and they could solve very hard problems and that is what made them good. So I don't frame that as top-down. I frame that as product leaders doing their job and product teams doing their job. It's a very common misunderstanding that many people have about what empowerment even means. Empowerment does not mean you set up this product team and they go decide what to work on. No, that would just be anarchy, right? You'd have 50 teams doing 50 things. Instead, empowerment means the leaders do their job, come up with the bets, and then the teams are able to figure out the best way to solve those problems.
turns.zh: 首先，我想说他所描述的现象正是我在优秀产品公司中所看到的，完全一致。但我们不把这视为自上而下的管理模式。自上而下实际上意味着完全不同的东西。事实上，把一份功能路线图交给团队，这就是典型的自上而下管理模式。另一个常见的误解，源于许多敏捷教练，他们误导了太多组织，但产品团队不负责制定产品战略。产品负责人负责制定产品战略，他们必须亲自承担这一职责。说实话，我对Meta（Facebook）并不是很欣赏，但扎克伯格在产品方面确实很出色。这正是当今行业的难题——他太擅长产品管理了。但这份工作本质上就是要做出战略决策、聚焦重点、下注于未来方向。但在优秀的组织中，你会把这些赌注交给团队，并赋予他们充分的自主权去解决问题。（00:46:08）说实话，我已经很久没有在Facebook工作了，但他们确实有很优秀的产品团队，跨职能协作出色，有很专业的工程师、产品经理和设计师，他们能够解决非常难的问题，这正是他们的成功之道。所以我不认为这是一种自上而下的管理模式。我认为这体现了产品负责人履行职责、产品团队发挥作用的本质。这是许多人对授权含义的误解。授权并不意味着你组建一个产品团队，让他们去决定要做什么。不然那就是无政府状态，对吧？你会有50个团队各自为政。相反，授权意味着领导者要做好本职工作，提出战略方向，然后让团队找到解决这些问题的最佳方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's a great clarification. I think a lot of people don't totally get that. So this is actually really helpful, I think, for a lot of people. Speaking of Meta, there's another product leader at Meta. He was actually one of the former guests and actually also one of the most popular episodes, Nikhyl Singhal. And he works with a lot of CPOs and heads of product at companies. The way he described it, he's noticed there's this reboot in what the PM role has been over the past couple of years because of the end of the [inaudible 00:47:31] era. So the way he sees it is for the past decade, PMs are mostly responsible as growth people. They're growing existing products, they have product market fit or they think they do and they're just optimizing, scaling. And now that the money has gone away, there's a return to building, finding product-market fit validation and discovery. I'm curious if you see that. Do you see a shift in what PMs should be doing in the last couple of years post [inaudible 00:47:58]?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这是一个非常清晰的解释。我觉得很多人都不是很理解这一点。所以我认为这对很多人来说真的很有帮助。说到Meta，还有一位在Meta的另一位产品负责人Nikhyl Singhal。他曾是我们节目的嘉宾，也是最受欢迎的嘉宾之一。他与许多公司的首席产品官和产品负责人合作。他指出，在过去几年里，由于[未听清00:47:31]时代的结束，产品经理的角色正在重新定义。在他看来，过去十年，产品经理主要负责增长业务。他们在现有产品上做优化，追求产品市场契合度或者自以为达到了这一目标，然后不断优化和扩规模。现在资金不再充裕，产品经理又回归到产品创新、验证产品市场契合度和探索新机会的阶段。我很好奇你是否也注意到了这一点。你是否也看到了过去几年[未听清00:47:58]后产品经理职责的转变？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: So yes and no. I think he's right in general, but there's a really important nuance. Many teams that aren't very good yet, they do exactly what he described. He describes as a gross hacking, I describe it as optimization. All they're doing is these low risk simple experiments. They live behind the AB test of just doing like, we're going to change the call to action here and maybe more people will register, that kind of test. Should they do that? Absolutely. Is that product really? Not really. That's not discovery, that's optimization. Now, in many companies they do that because they're given a roadmap of all the features. So all they can really fit in are these little optimization tests. But in others, they're scared to do anything else. They literally don't want to break it. And so I find that situation that he described in many companies that need to transform. (00:48:58): So I would argue what he's probably seeing mostly is a team that's learning how to go from a feature team to a product team. Now, has that happened more in the last two years? I would like to believe so, but I don't know. Some days I feel like yes, he's right. Some days I feel like I don't know who he's talking to because these people are still stuck doing optimization work. And so there's probably a lot of nuance there. In general, I think yes, but I don't think it's tied to interest rates. I don't think it's tied to that. I think it's more tied to the quality of the leadership and the need of the business to do more than optimization.
turns.zh:
是的，也不是。我认为他总体上是对的，但这里有个很重要的细微差别。许多尚未强大起来的团队，他们正是按照他所描述的方式行事。他称之为"粗暴的黑客行为"，我则称之为"优化"。他们所做的不过是这些低风险的简单实验。他们躲在AB测试的庇护下，比如"我们要改动这里的行动呼吁，或许就能吸引更多注册用户"之类的测试。这样做对吗？当然对。但这真的是产品创新吗？并非如此。这不是探索创新，而是优化现有方案。如今许多公司之所以这么做，是因为他们拿到了详尽的功能路线图，所以只能塞进这些小优化测试。但其他团队则害怕尝试新事物，生怕把事情搞砸。我发现他所描述的这种情况，在许多需要变革的公司中普遍存在。  

（00:48:58）：所以我认为他所观察到的大多是团队正在从功能团队向产品团队转型。近两年这种情况是否更常见？我愿意相信是这样，但我也不确定。有时我觉得他说得对，有时又觉得他说得不对，因为这些人仍深陷优化工作中。所以这里可能存在诸多微妙之处。总体而言，我认为是的，但我认为这与利率无关。我认为这更多地与领导层的素质以及业务对超越优化的需求相关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know people ask you this all the time, but I'm curious, is there anything big you're seeing change in the PM role broadly?
turns.zh: 我知道人们总问你这个问题，但我很好奇，PM角色的整体变化中是否有重大趋势？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: We've talked about quite a few big dynamics that are changing. Interestingly, what we're really been talking about is the different definitions of the PM role. And so if we hold one of those definitions constant, let's say we are focused now on the empowered product manager, the one you and I grew up with, and those are the ones that are responsible for value and viability. In general, I think the principles are stable and I think they will remain stable. However, the techniques are undergoing some radical changes, especially with generative AI. Don't get me wrong, I've been living this every day as most of us have. I don't have it figured out. In fact, I recently changed my advice because I used to say, start with ChatGPT, go from there and I'll help you make that great. We'll go from there. (00:50:48): And what I kept seeing was people taking what they get too literally, too seriously, too much value, and they were heading off in a wrong direction and then they were optimizing that. There's a lot going on right now. It's a moving target. Depends which system you're using and the day of the week now on what you're at, but whatever. Now I've been recommending to people that they think through the answer first. Really get them to think, put something down, then use ChatGPT to see if you can't improve on that, to see if you can't challenge that, to see if you can't make your argument tighter. So I've reversed and I did that because people are trusting the results too much.
turns.zh: 我们讨论过不少正在变化的关键动态。有趣的是，我们真正探讨的是PM角色的不同定义。假设我们固定其中一种定义——比如我们现在关注的是赋权型产品经理，也就是你我成长过程中所熟知的角色，负责价值创造和产品可行性的人。总体而言，我认为这些原则是稳定的，也会继续稳定。但技术手段正在经历剧烈变革，尤其是生成式AI。别误会，我和大多数人一样每天都在应对这些挑战。我还没想清楚。事实上，最近我调整了建议——我曾说从ChatGPT入手，逐步优化。但我发现很多人把结果看得太字面、太严肃，赋予其过多价值，结果走入歧途，然后又开始优化。这里有很多动态变化。这是个移动的目标。取决于你使用的系统和当天的工作进度，但无所谓了。现在我建议人们先仔细思考答案。真正让他们思考，写下思路，然后用ChatGPT看看能否改进，能否挑战现有观点，能否让论点更严密。所以我改变了策略，因为人们太依赖结果了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you talk about what they start with, is it like, here's a strategy I'm thinking for this product, or is it like a PRD [inaudible 00:51:48]
turns.zh: 你说他们从哪里开始，是先制定产品策略，还是先写PRD [00:51:48，语音不清]？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Yeah, certainly you can use it for a spec, a PRD. You can certainly use it for strategy. You can certainly use it for even things like triaging bugs. It's hard to think of something you can't use it for. The harder question is what is it good for?
turns.zh: 是的，当然你可以用它来做规格说明、产品需求文档（PRD），做战略规划，甚至用来处理问题追踪之类的事情。很难想象有什么事情不能用它来做。但更难的问题是，它到底有什么实际用处？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something along those lines I wanted to chat about. Something I've been thinking about. I want to write a post about this, is which skills of a product manager will be most disrupted by AI? So I think short term, there's communication is getting improved. You can improve your writing strategy. Maybe like here's my strategy, give me some feedback. So I think things are being optimized a bit through ChatGPT and tools like that. But in the five or 10 years, are there any skills that will potentially go away or 95% of it will be done by AI? And if so, where do you see most of that change happening in the skillsets?
turns.zh: 这正是我想聊聊的点。最近我一直在思考这个问题。我想写一篇关于产品经理哪些技能会被AI颠覆的文章。短期来看，沟通能力确实在提升。你可以优化写作策略。比如说："这是我的策略，请给我反馈。"通过ChatGPT和类似工具，沟通效率确实有所提升。但五年或十年后，是否会有95%的技能被AI取代？如果真是这样，你认为这些技能变革主要会出现在哪些领域？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Absolutely. And I think that is happening more on the engineering side right now and also on the design side, but I fully expect it will happen. Like I said at the beginning, I don't know when really because that timing is hard question, but this is another one of my arguments to people of why you need to uplevel your skills. If you are fundamentally a backlog administrator, good luck protecting that because already people are doing that. It's only a matter of time before that becomes pretty well-supported. That is not a good job prospect. Now, then we can talk about a feature team, project manager. There's very little that's going on in there that is truly value add. Most of these are administrative kinds of things that can be done at least significantly with help. So I wouldn't feel confident if I was a feature team product manager that I could keep doing this for any amount of years at least. (00:53:45): Now, for an empowered product manager, if your responsibility is value and viability, if you boil it down, that's the real challenge left with ChatGPT or GenAI, is viability becomes even more the important question. There's some very hard things left. So designers, I think the real product designers at the top of the chain, they're going to be incredibly important and of course tech leads are going to be incredibly important more than ever. But for a product manager, especially with viability, I've been on so many of these calls where we've been talking about the implications of probabilistic software versus deterministic software and what is okay? The lawyers are weighing in already with the legal perspective, but also ethical perspective and just if this is mission critical, is this something that we could be okay with having a probabilistic answer? (00:54:49): We don't know, trying to figure that out. So what is that really? That's a viability and a value question. So a lot more is landing squarely on the product manager than I think in general in the past.
turns.zh:
当然。我认为这在工程和设计领域已经有所体现，但我坚信这种趋势还会持续下去。正如我开头所说，我不知道具体时间点，因为这很难预测。但这也让我更坚定地认为，你需要不断提升自己的技能。如果你本质上只是个待办事项管理员，那就好运吧，因为已经有人在做这件事了。这类工作迟早会被自动化取代。这可不是个好的职业前景。现在再谈谈产品团队和项目经理。产品团队和项目经理的工作中，真正有价值增值的部分很少。大部分都是行政性工作，至少在一定程度上可以借助工具完成。所以如果我是产品经理，我不确定自己能否在未来几年里一直胜任这份工作。
(00:53:45): 对于有能力的产品经理来说，如果你的职责是价值和可行性，那么归根结底，这才是ChatGPT或GenAI带来的真正挑战——可行性问题将变得更加重要。还有一些非常难解决的挑战。比如设计师，特别是顶尖设计师，他们将变得极其重要。当然，技术负责人也比以往任何时候都更加重要。但对于产品经理来说，特别是关于可行性，我参加过很多这样的会议，我们讨论了概率性软件与确定性软件的差异，以及什么是可以接受的。律师们已经从法律和伦理角度参与进来，但如果这关乎关键任务，我们能接受概率性解决方案吗？(00:54:49): 我们还不知道，这确实是个难题。所以这到底是什么？这是一个可行性和价值的问题。因此，相较于过去，产品经理需要承担更多责任。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you talk about viability, just so people know what you mean when you say that? What's the one sentence definition of what viability means?
turns.zh: 你能谈谈可行性吗？让大家明白你说的“可行性”具体指什么？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: So value means for the customer, viability means for your business. So that means it works for your business. You can sell it, market it. It's legal, you can service it. It's compliance. All of these constraints. Remember Airbnb, it wasn't so hard to get people to sign up. It was hard to make listings legal in San Francisco. That's the hard part, is the compliance side.
turns.zh: 因此，对客户而言，价值意味着可行性；对你的业务而言，价值意味着可持续性。这意味着它对你的业务切实可行。你可以将其销售、推广。它合法合规，你能提供相关服务。这就是合规性所带来的诸多限制。记得Airbnb吗？让人们注册并不难，但要让房源在旧金山合法化却困难重重。这才是真正的挑战——合规性方面的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about your book. Is there anything else along these lines before we get into your book that you thought would be interesting to touch on or share?
turns.zh: 我想谈谈你的书。在深入探讨你的书之前，是否有其他相关话题你认为值得提及或分享？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: I think that's good. We covered a lot. We covered a lot.
turns.zh: 我觉得今天已经讨论得够多了。我们聊了很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We did. I imagine we covered some of the elements of your book, but let's talk about the book. So this is your third book, is that right?
turns.zh: 确实如此。我想我们已经涉及了你书中的一些要点，但还是来聊聊这本书吧。据我所知，这是你的第三本书，对吧？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What made you decide to write another book and add an addition to the Marty Cagan cannon and what is it about?
turns.zh: 好的。是什么促使你决定再写一本书，扩充马蒂·卡根的著作体系？这本书主要讲什么？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: This is a different one though. It's different kind because INSPIRED, hopefully you know, is for product teams and product managers. It's really a book about product discovery. And then EMPOWER is really about product leadership, vision strategy, team topology, coaching. It's all about that. And that was the original idea. We would share those techniques 'cause that's what we share. But the single most common question we got honestly from the first edition of INSPIRED was that people would read the book and they would say, I love this, I want to do this. But have you ever seen our company? We are so far away from that. We are like night and day. And in fact, a lot of people would tell me point blank, there's no way their company's going to go along with this. And so what they were asking was, how in the world do you transform to work like this? (00:57:01): And we've been getting that question for years now. That's really what my partners, Christian, Jonathan, Christopher, Leah, that's what they do is they help companies to transform. That's what we've been doing. But we do that on a one-off basis. There's only five of us. How many companies could we possibly work with? So we realized that this question was a global question. And if we've written books that explain, maybe you want to work this way, but we don't address how to change to work this way, that's leaving people without that hard part. So the goal of TRANSFORMED, unlike the other books, was to share how to actually change. There are techniques in TRANSFORMED as well, but there are transformation techniques. There are change techniques like the use of pilot teams or spreading things out to divide and conquer on some of the transformation work. (00:58:01): So the other thing we wanted to do, in fact, we made a rule for ourselves. We knew we needed lots of examples, case studies, but we said it's too easy to include Silicon Valley companies because Airbnb was born in this model. They were designers, but still they were a Silicon Valley company. It was a big advantage for Airbnb over say your favorite bank or whatever that was not born in this way of working. So we said all our examples are going to be from outside Silicon Valley world. They're all companies, most of them pre-internet, that had to change dramatically to work this way. And not only were we going to show how they changed, but we were going to show what they were able to do when they changed, which to me is the coolest part, seeing the innovation. Some of these innovations, honestly, Lenny, are as impressive as anything I've seen Amazon do and that's saying a lot. (00:58:59): Amazon in my opinion is the top of the pack and so that's impressive, what Trainline in the UK was able to do. A company I had never known before a few years ago in Saudi Arabia called Almosafer, a travel agency. They own, I forget what it is, 80 plus percent of the market over Expedia, over the big guys in the US because they actually learned this stuff and were able to do it. And we have a dozen examples from all over the world, Brazil, Virginia, everywhere, not Silicon Valley. In healthcare and car sales and fitness, all over the place. Honestly there was a few reasons. One is we wanted them to understand what it really means to move to this way of working. No fluff, just what does it really mean? Otherwise, how are they going to get there if they don't even know where there is? Then we wanted them to believe it's possible to transform. We're the first ones to say it's not easy, but we wanted them to believe it's possible. (01:00:10): And the third thing is we wanted to get them excited about what they'd be able to do after they transformed. And those were the three things we were trying to do in the book. And so that's different than our other books, but hopefully it makes the other books more accessible. They'll be able to apply more of them.
turns.zh:
不过这本书有所不同。《INSPIRED》（灵感）这本书面向产品团队和产品经理，重点在于产品探索；而《EMPOWER》则聚焦产品领导力、愿景战略、团队架构和教练指导。这正是我们最初的创作初衷。我们会分享这些技巧，因为这正是我们一直致力于做的。但在《INSPIRED》第一版发行后，我们收到最多的反馈是，读者读完书后会说："我很喜欢这些理念，也想实践这些方法，但看看我们公司的情况，差距实在太大了。"事实上，很多读者直言不讳地表示，他们的公司根本不可能采纳这些理念。于是他们追问："到底要如何才能实现这样的转变？"（00:57:01）  
多年来，我们不断收到这样的疑问。这正是我的合作伙伴克里斯蒂安、乔纳森、克里斯托弗和莉亚所专注的方向——帮助企业实现转型。这是我们一直致力于的目标。但我们只能一次性服务五家公司，覆盖的企业数量实在有限。因此我们意识到，这个问题具有普适性。我们过去的书籍只是解释"你应该如何工作"，却忽略了"如何实现转变"的关键环节。因此《TRANSFORMED》（转型）这本书的核心目标是分享具体的转型方法。书中同样包含技巧，但重点在于变革策略，比如试点团队、分阶段推进等创新手段。  
（00:58:01）  
另外，我们制定了一条原则：案例必须来自硅谷以外。亚马逊虽然诞生于这种模式，但其本质仍是硅谷公司。这对亚马逊而言是巨大优势，而其他传统企业（比如你最喜欢的银行）却无法轻易复制这种模式。因此，我们精心挑选了全球各地的非硅谷企业作为案例研究对象。这些公司大多诞生于互联网时代之前，却通过彻底变革实现了创新。最令人惊叹的案例包括：  
• 英国的Trainline——几年前我从未听说过这家公司，但它通过学习这些方法成功挑战了Expedia等巨头  
• 沙特阿拉伯的Almosafer旅行社——仅凭借这些方法就占据了80%以上的市场份额  
• 巴西、弗吉尼亚等地的创新实践  
• 医疗、汽车销售、健身等领域的变革  

这些案例的共同点在于：让读者直观理解转型的本质——不是空谈理论，而是实战指南；让他们相信变革的可能性——我们率先承认这条路不易，但要传递信心。（01:00:10）  

---
第三件事是，我们想让他们对变身后能做什么感到兴奋。这就是我们在这本书中努力实现的三个目标。这与我们其他书籍的写作思路有所不同，但希望这能让其他书籍更易于理解，读者也能更好地将书中的知识应用到实际生活中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who would you say this is most suited for? Is it leaders at companies? Is it ICPMs, everybody? Who do you think would get the most out of this?
turns.zh: 你觉得这本书最适合谁？是公司的领导层吗？是产品经理吗？还是所有人？你觉得谁能从中获得最大收益？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: We wrote it intentionally, again, unlike the other books. The other books are written for people like us and your audience and my audience. They're product people. These are written for non-product people too. And so the idea is a CEO, a CFO, a head of sale. Anybody who cares about their company changing how they build and wants to help is written for them. So that was one of the hardest parts really, including those kinds of reviewers and making sure all this stuff made sense to them.
turns.zh: 我们特意这么写的，和其他书不同。其他书是为像我们这样的人写的，为你的读者和我的读者写的。他们是产品人员。但这本书也为非产品人员写的。所以目标读者是CEO、CFO、销售负责人。任何关心公司如何变革产品建设并愿意助力的人。我们写这本书时，最困难的部分之一就是要让那些类型的评论者理解，并确保所有内容对他们来说都通顺易懂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So basically if you're listening to this and you're like, I'm working on these teams Marty's describing, I don't think this is optimal. We can do a lot better. We can get a lot more on out feature team, hand this book to your CEO essentially?
turns.zh: 所以基本上，如果你听了这段内容，心里想，"我在马蒂描述的这些团队里工作，我觉得这并不理想。我们能做得更好。在我们的功能团队中能获得更多收获，把这本书交给你的CEO如何？"

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: And I'd suggest they read it themselves so they know. Because I know I'm going to be talking more about this going forward because I know I need to. Too many people in our industry view themselves as a victim of their company. They're stuck in a feature team and there's nothing they can do about it other than quit. But really they have a family, they're not going to quit. So I think that's not true. I think there is so much they can do and hopefully they can see that in the book. It's like they can see what they individually can do to push their company in this direction, and at a minimum it'll help their career.
turns.zh: 我建议他们自己读一读，这样他们就能明白了。因为我知道我未来会更多地谈论这个话题，因为我觉得有必要。我们的行业里太多人把自己视为公司的受害者。他们被困在功能团队里，除了辞职别无他法。但实际上他们有家庭，不会辞职。所以我认为这不是事实。我认为他们能做很多事，希望他们能在书中看到这一点。比如，他们能看到自己可以为推动公司朝这个方向发展做些什么，至少这能对他们的职业生涯有所帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I always love just the message of empowerment and giving people motivation to you can actually make change. You're not stuck in this way of working, and I know you do that a lot. The official title of the book, so it's TRANSFORMED: Moving to the Product Operating Model. What do you mean when you... There it is. I don't have my copy yet 'cause that hasn't come out in the US yet, otherwise, I'd have it here on my side as well. There it is. It's a beautiful green color by the way. It goes nicely with the other colors. Amazing. Beautiful design, whoever did that. Okay, so the part of the title is Moving to the Product Operating Model. What does that mean?
turns.zh: 我一直很喜欢赋予人们力量、给他们动力这样一个理念，让他们知道自己其实可以带来改变。你不必被困在这种工作方式中，我知道你经常这样做。书的正式书名是《转型：向产品运营模式迈进》。书名中的“TRANSFORMED”是什么意思？就在这儿。我还没拿到美国版的书，否则我也会把它放在身边。书名是绿色的，很漂亮，和其他颜色很搭。太棒了。设计得真美，不管是谁设计的。好的，书名部分是“向产品运营模式迈进”。这意味着什么？

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: That was the biggest pain for the book was... 'Cause honestly, I had dodged that question for 20 years. If you look at any of my writing before starting on this book, I just said, "Look, do you want to work like the best or do you want to work like the rest?" That's how we referred to it, the best versus the rest because there is no word, there is no name that talks about the common principles with all the best companies. So we would just say, do you want to work like the best or not? But when I started to write the book, I'm like, okay, I can't just say work like the best. We have to have some name for this, but I don't know if you've come across this Lenny, but you don't want to coin a new term if you can avoid it. (01:03:27): It is really painful to try to develop a new term. Some of the companies we worked with use the term product operating model and don't get me wrong, that's not the only term. Some people use the term product led company or product driven company, but those two we just don't like because it gives all the wrong message and the rest of the company thinks it's a power grab. So we wanted to avoid those words. We like product operating model for a couple reasons. One is it's a model, it's a conceptual model. It's not a process. It's not really a thing, it's more of a set of principles and also it's non-threatening to a lot of people. It's just saying, "Look, this is how these companies operate. You can look at it and decide if you think it's good for you too." So we adopted that term, we call it product model for short. And all it really is it boils down to a set of 20 principles and those 20 principles are what we find. (01:04:36): Remember we started with this. I was explaining, when I listen to your guests, I'm listening for what's special about each of their companies, but what I'm looking for is the commonality. 'Cause most of the time when I see a successful company, they are living these principles. Principles like you have to experiment. You have to embrace experimentation. If you don't do that, most of this is not possible. Or you have to make sure that everything you release is instrumented so that we can prove the outcome. Stuff like that, that there's a million different methodologies and frameworks and tools and processes, but matters is those principles. And so that's what we mean by that product operating model. There's at a high level we talk about it, is how you decide what you're going to work on? How you decide which problems to solve? (01:05:33): That's what most companies do in annual planning, but it's basically the product strategy. That's what your Meta friend was describing that the leaders do. That's their job. The second is how do they solve problems? Do they have the skills to do product discovery like we're talking about? How to actually come up with good solutions that work for the customer and work for the business. That's the second big dimension of the product model. And the third big dimension is how do they actually build, test and deploy product to their customers? Do they do it in a way that is reliable, that is demonstrable where you can show that this generates the outcomes that you need? Those are the three big areas. And then there's a number of competencies. There's four new competencies that most companies don't have, but what makes it tricky is they have people with those titles, but they don't have people with those jobs. The one we've been talking about is product manager.
turns.zh: 写这本书最头疼的地方在于……说实话，我回避这个问题已经20年了。如果你看看我在这本书之前的写作内容，我只是说："听着，你是想像最优秀的公司那样工作，还是想随大流？"我们当时就是这么说的，"最优秀的公司" versus "随大流的公司"，因为没有一个词、一个名称能概括所有顶尖公司的共同原则。所以我们就直接问：你想不想像最优秀的公司那样工作？但当我开始写这本书时，我想，好吧，我不能只说"像最优秀的公司那样工作"。我们得给这个概念起个名字，但不知道你有没有注意到，莱尼，如果可以避免的话，最好别创造新术语。（01:03:27）：开发一个新术语真的很痛苦。我们合作过的有些公司用"产品运营模式"这个术语，但别误会，这不是唯一的术语。有些人用"产品主导型公司"或"产品驱动型公司"，但这两个词我们都不喜欢，因为它们传递了错误的信息，其他部门会认为这是在夺权。所以我们想避免这些词汇。我们喜欢"产品运营模式"有几个原因。首先，它是一个模型，是一个概念模型。它不是一个流程，也不是一个具体的东西，而是更像一套原则，而且对很多人来说无害。它只是说："看看，这些公司是这么运作的。你可以研究一下，看看对你们是否适用。"所以我们采用了这个术语，简称"产品模式"。归根结底，它只归结为20条原则，而这些原则正是我们发现的。（01:04:36）：记得我们一开始讨论这个问题时。我在听你们的嘉宾发言时，会留意他们公司的独特之处，但我更关注共性部分。因为大多数成功的公司都在践行这些原则。比如，你必须进行实验。你必须接纳实验的文化。如果不这样做，大多数事情都无法实现。或者你必须确保发布的每一项成果都经过数据验证，这样我们才能证明其效果。这类原则还有无数不同的方法论、框架、工具和流程，但关键在于这些原则。所以这就是我们所说的产品运营模式。在高层层面，我们讨论的是：你如何决定要做什么？你如何决定要解决哪些问题？（01:05:33）：这就是大多数公司在年度规划中做的事情，但这本质上是产品战略。正如你们的Meta朋友所描述的，领导者要做的事情。这是他们的职责。其次，他们如何解决问题？他们是否具备我们所说的产品探索能力？如何真正想出对客户和业务都有效的解决方案？这是产品模式的第二大维度。第三大维度是他们如何实际构建、测试并向客户部署产品？他们是否以可靠、可验证的方式进行，确保能产生所需的结果？这就是三个主要领域。然后还有一系列能力。大多数公司没有的四项新能力，但困难之处在于，他们有这些职位头衔的人，但没有真正从事这些工作的人。我们一直在讨论的那个职位就是产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What would be most interesting to share? You said there's 20 attributes of a power product team.
turns.zh: 分享最有趣的内容是什么？你说一个强大的产品团队有20项特质。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: 20 principles.
turns.zh: 20项原则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 20 principles. I'm so curious what these are, but I know we don't have time to go through them all. Can you either share a few of those? You shared experimentation as one, or these four what you just mentioned. I'm just curious what these [inaudible 01:06:58]
turns.zh: 20项原则。我很好奇这些具体是什么，但我们没时间一一探讨。你能不能分享其中几项？你提到了实验精神，还有你刚刚提到的四项。我很好奇其他的（01:10:58，语音不清）

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: Well, I could share as much as you want, but the four competencies are product manager. Again, we're talking a serious product manager here, not a product owner, not a feature team product manager. Product manager, real product designer, service design, interaction design, visual design, user research, real product designer, a real tech lead, and then a real product leader, a manager of product design engineering that knows how to coach their people and knows how to do a real product strategy, which is what we were talking about. So those are the four new competencies. For most companies, those are new, meaning they might have people with those names, but they don't have those roles institutionalized.
turns.zh: 嗯，你想让我分享多少都可以，但这四项核心能力指的是产品经理。再强调一下，我们说的是真正的产品经理，不是产品负责人，也不是功能团队的产品经理。产品经理、真正的产品设计师、服务设计、交互设计、视觉设计、用户研究、真正的产品设计师、真正的技术负责人，还有真正的产品负责人，即懂如何指导团队、制定真正产品战略的产品设计工程管理者。这就是我们所说的四项新能力。对于大多数公司来说，这些都是新概念，可能有相应头衔的人，但这些角色并未被制度化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, you're building on the classic triad with this leader above. It's like the stool with something on the stool or something or filling up the stool.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，你在现有经典三角结构基础上进行了拓展。这就像凳子上放东西，或者填满凳子。

turns.speaker: Marty Cagan
turns.en: And that is the triad. That's where it came from. The word triad came from those three. We didn't invent that.
turns.zh: 这就是三角结构的本质。三角结构源自这三个角色，我们并非首创这个概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
